title: Agent Builder's Playbook — Sep 15, 2026
intro: This edition leans structural: five of six cards replace a prompt-level or per-deployment shortcut — a shared API key, prompt-only exfiltration rules, a name-based eval baseline — with a traceable system that holds up under scale or attack.

cards.title: Decouple test-selector state from processing to survive CI's growth curve
cards.problem: Anthropic's CI job volume grew 25x in six months as Claude wrote 80% of shipped code, and the singleton listener-plus-selector service behind test impact analysis couldn't scale past that.
cards.apply: Split the test-selection service into stateless listener workers that append results to a journal, a separate consumer that rolls journal entries into test history, and a selector that queries that store — instead of one process holding state and picking tests together.
cards.result: The old architecture needed a new stopgap patch every 24–70 days as load grew; the decoupled redesign has kept the backlog flat with no recurring strain since.

evidence.note: Anthropic reports the patch-lifespan and post-redesign backlog figures from its own CI system.

cards.title: Resolve OAuth credentials per caller, not per deployment, in shared agents
cards.problem: A single shared API key answers what an agent may do but not who asked, so every action a multi-tenant agent takes lands under one service account regardless of which user triggered it.
cards.apply: Split credentials into agent-owned (one static secret shared by every caller) and user-owned (an OAuth grant resolved per caller at runtime via a single connections.get() call), and batch every missing grant into one consent pause before the first model turn instead of prompting mid-run.
cards.result: LangChain reports tool actions now carry the actual caller's identity in the same deployment — tickets show the real user's handle and private-repo visibility differs per caller — with no code changes per user.

evidence.note: LangChain describes the behavior qualitatively; no quantitative metrics are given.

cards.title: Separate quality drift from infrastructure failure with a two-layer monitor
cards.problem: A production agent can call every tool without error and still misunderstand the user, and a revoked IAM permission can return an empty response instead of an exception — so quality problems and infrastructure failures look identical from outside.
cards.apply: Run an LLM-as-judge layer that asynchronously samples live requests and scores helpfulness, correctness, and goal success without added latency, alongside an autonomous investigator that reads infrastructure logs, builds a resource topology graph, and correlates errors across IAM, model, and runtime to name the specific broken permission or resource.
cards.result: AWS reports its airline-reservation case study shows the infrastructure layer isolating a missing bedrock:InvokeModel permission as root cause, keeping it distinct from a quality regression the judge layer would otherwise lump it with.

evidence.note: AWS walks through a worked case study; no comparative detection-time or false-positive metrics are reported.

cards.title: Enforce data-exfiltration blocks at the tool layer, not the prompt
cards.problem: An agent with read access to internal data (Slack, Kubernetes, analytics), live internet access, and write access to a public repo — the 'lethal trifecta' — can leak sensitive internal details into a public commit with no human in the loop to catch it.
cards.apply: Add a policy engine that tracks which internal sources an agent has read in a session and blocks, before execution, any tool call that would publish that data to a public destination — combining rule-based checks with LLM classification rather than relying on prompt instructions to hold.
cards.result: Archestra reports this closes the exposure the trifecta creates, on the reasoning that prompt instructions are only as reliable as the model's mood.

evidence.note: Archestra describes its own policy-engine mitigation; no incident metrics or false-positive rate are given.

cards.title: Track an agent's behavioral identity, not its name, across eval and deployment
cards.problem: Prompt edits, tool-schema changes, model fallbacks, and routing tweaks can drift a deployed agent away from the version that passed evaluation, so the agent in production may no longer be the one that was tested — while still answering to the same name.
cards.apply: Bind certification to a specific tracked revision instead of a name: record the context sources, policies, and capabilities each production action actually used, so any run can be replayed to show what governed it, even without deterministic outputs.
cards.result: This closes the gap where a config change silently invalidates an eval result, because certification, authorization, and audit all point at the exact behavior that ran rather than just a label.

evidence.note: The source proposes this as a framework, not a measured before/after result.

cards.title: Mine historical attention scores to compress RAG context instead of compressing per query
cards.problem: RAG's longer contexts raise latency, KV-cache memory, and token cost, and most per-query compression methods add enough overhead to offset the savings they create.
cards.apply: Build a document-keyed store of importance scores mined from the generator's historical attention traces across repeated document accesses, then generate a budget-specific plain-text view of each retrieved document from that store instead of running a fresh compression pass on every query.
cards.result: REVA reports 1.0–5.8 points higher generation quality than existing compression methods, 5.3–15.6x lower compression overhead, and under 40ms of added latency across four benchmarks.

evidence.note: The paper reports these as benchmarked results across four evaluation sets against existing compression methods.
